name: time-series-iot
context: Thousands of devices emit millions of timestamped samples on periodic schedules, into a schema that is defined by the fleet rather than by a single designer, where series are strongly correlated, records arrive late, and the dominant queries are range aggregations rather than point lookups. The pattern stores data in a time-oriented model with a tree/path identity, columnar chunks grouped so that one device's chunks sit together, multi-level statistics so an aggregation can be answered without scanning raw points, and a tiered rollup structure so a multi-year archive costs gigabytes rather than the tens of terabytes of raw retention.
benefits: Columnar, chunk-per-time-range layout makes time-range scans cheap and lets closed chunks be compressed aggressively
Chunk groups co-locate one device's chunks in contiguous disk space because those chunks are almost always queried together
Page, chunk and file-level statistics let an aggregation answer from metadata alone when the data is immutable
A tree/path data model absorbs device-defined, ever-evolving schema without a migration per fleet
Tiered rollups with per-tier retention keep long-range history cheap while the raw window stays short
tradeoffs: Rollup correctness depends on the raw retention window strictly exceeding the widest aggregate's refresh reach, or buckets materialise empty and the history is gone
Aggregate storage scales with series cardinality, not with the raw sample rate — cardinality is the cost driver
Late and out-of-order arrivals complicate ingestion ordering and force write paths that tolerate delayed data
High-frequency ingestion demands a specialised write path; general-purpose databases pay for generality
Aggregates introduce lag: recent data is only in the rollup once the refresh job has run
use_cases: Industrial sensor fleets with thousands of devices and millions of correlated measurements
Fleet telemetry for vehicles, meters and machines emitting on a fixed sampling schedule
Long-horizon trend analysis where raw retention is expensive and rollups answer the query
IoT analytics requiring both real-time queries over recent data and batch analysis over years
Edge deployments that collect locally, synchronise files, and query the same model in the cloud
avoid_when: The data is not time-ordered in any meaningful way, so the time axis buys nothing
Point lookups by primary key dominate rather than range aggregations
Cardinality is unbounded (a tag value per reading) and no cardinality budget can be enforced
The workload is small and a general-purpose relational database with partitioning is sufficient
component_types: Time-series model: tree or path identity so schema evolves with the fleet rather than through migrations
Columnar chunk: time-ordered, encoded and compressed block of data points for one series
Chunk group: chunks of one or more series of a device written in the same period, stored contiguously
Statistics tiers: page, chunk and file level summaries used to skip raw reads in aggregation
Downsampling / continuous aggregate: coarser rollup refreshed incrementally in the background
Retention policy: per-tier drop boundary that discards expired chunks automatically
Cardinality guard: control over the number of distinct series a measurement and tag set creates
anti_patterns: Putting an unbounded value (a user id, a request id) in an indexed tag, causing runaway series cardinality
Setting the raw retention window shorter than an aggregate's refresh start_offset, so rollups materialise empty buckets
Aggregating averages of averages, which silently corrupts the result when bucket populations differ
Attaching one global retention policy to data with genuinely different retention requirements per tenant
Treating the raw store as the only tier, then paying full raw storage cost for a five-year archive
design_principles: Time is the primary axis of both storage and query
Store statistics alongside data so aggregates do not have to read it
Aggregate storage cost is governed by cardinality, not volume
Retention is layered: raw is short, rollups are long, and the boundary follows the query horizon
Schemas belong to the fleet, so the data model must tolerate unknown series appearing
best_practices: Compute cardinality before modelling: worst case is tag keys times tag values times field keys
Keep the raw retention window several times wider than the widest aggregate refresh reach, with margin for scheduler lag
Re-aggregate sums and counts at every level and derive averages from them rather than averaging rollups
Give each tier its own retention policy and verify the oldest surviving data matches the horizon
Compress closed chunks on a schedule; typical sensor data compresses by an order of magnitude
references: InfluxData, Designing Your Schema — measurements, tags, fields, buckets, retention and cardinality, https://awesome.influxdata.com/docs/part-2/designing-your-schema/
Apache IoTDB, Time-Series Data Model — device-defined evolving schema and correlated series, https://iotdb.apache.org/UserGuide/latest/Basic-Concept/Time-Series-Model.html
TimescaleDB, Hypertables — automatic time-based chunking, compression and retention, https://docs.timescale.com/use-timescale/latest/hypertables/
Apache Kafka, Core Concepts — event time as the clock for late-arriving IoT records, https://kafka.apache.org/43/streams/core-concepts/
